title: Unit 6: Funds & Fees
subtitle: Index funds, ETFs, and keeping costs low

questions.prompt: What is an index fund?
choices: A fund that buys all (or a representative sample of) the stocks in a market index
A fund where a manager hand-picks a few stocks hoping to beat the market
A savings account that tracks inflation
A single company's stock
questions.explanation: An index fund simply mirrors an index, like the S&P 500, so you own a little piece of everything in it.

questions.prompt: An index fund's goal is to match the market's return, not to beat it.
questions.explanation: By copying the index instead of trying to outsmart it, index funds aim for the market's average return at very low cost.

questions.prompt: The S&P 500 is an index made up of roughly what?
choices: 500 of the largest U.S. companies
500 cryptocurrencies
50 government bonds
5,000 global startups
questions.explanation: The S&P 500 tracks about 500 of the biggest U.S. companies, so an S&P 500 index fund spreads your money across all of them.

questions.prompt: Which of these are real advantages of index funds? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Instant diversification across many companies
Low costs because there's no expensive stock-picking team
A guarantee that you'll never lose money
They have historically beaten most active funds over the long run
questions.explanation: Index funds are cheap, diversified, and beat most active funds over time — but no investment can promise you'll never lose money.

questions.prompt: The S&P 500 index is built from 500 companies. Owning one share of a fund that tracks it gives you a slice of how many companies?
questions.explanation: One share of an S&P 500 index fund spreads your money across all 500 companies at once — that's diversification in a single click.

questions.prompt: Because most active fund managers fail to beat their index over the long run, a low-cost index fund is often a smart default.
questions.explanation: Study after study shows the large majority of active managers lag their benchmark after fees, which is why index funds are so popular.

questions.prompt: Order these from least diversified to most diversified.
items: A total U.S. market index fund (thousands of companies)
questions.explanation: The more companies you hold, the more spread out your risk — going from one stock to a total-market fund steadily increases diversification.

questions.prompt: What's a key difference in how ETFs and mutual funds trade?
choices: ETFs trade throughout the day like a stock; mutual funds price just once per day after the market closes
Mutual funds trade every second; ETFs trade only once a year
There is no difference between them
ETFs can only be bought by banks
questions.explanation: ETF (exchange-traded fund) prices move all day like a stock, while a mutual fund settles at one price after the close.

questions.prompt: Sort each trait into ETF or Mutual Fund.
items: You can buy or sell it anytime the market is open
Your order fills at the closing NAV price
Traded through a brokerage using a ticker symbol
Often has a minimum initial investment, like $1,000 or $3,000
questions.explanation: ETFs act like stocks with live pricing and a ticker; mutual funds price once daily at NAV and frequently require a minimum to start.

questions.prompt: If you place a mutual fund order at 11 a.m., it is executed instantly at that moment's live price.
questions.explanation: Mutual fund orders all fill at the same day-end NAV, no matter what time of day you place them.

questions.prompt: What are fractional shares?
choices: Buying a portion of a share, so you can invest a set dollar amount even when one whole share is expensive
Shares that are broken and can't be sold
A share that pays no dividends
Free shares handed out by the government
questions.explanation: Fractional shares let you invest, say, $50 in a fund even if one full share costs hundreds — great for starting small.

questions.prompt: Which statements about ETFs are TRUE? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: They trade throughout the day
Many track an index, just like index mutual funds
They usually have a ticker symbol you can look up
They can only be sold once a year
questions.explanation: ETFs trade live all day, carry a ticker, and often track indexes — you're never locked in to selling just once a year.

questions.prompt: Both ETFs and mutual funds let you own a basket of many investments in a single purchase.
questions.explanation: Whichever wrapper you pick, one purchase buys a whole basket of holdings — instant diversification.

questions.prompt: One share of a fund costs $250, but you only want to invest $50. How many shares do you buy? (Enter as a decimal.)
questions.explanation: $50 divided by $250 is 0.2 — fractional shares let you put in exactly the dollar amount you want.

questions.prompt: What are a fund's "holdings"?
choices: The individual investments, like stocks, that the fund owns
The fees the fund charges you
The number of investors in the fund
The bank that stores the fund
questions.explanation: A fund's holdings are simply the list of companies (or bonds) it owns on your behalf.

questions.prompt: Match each company to the sector it belongs to.
questions.explanation: Funds group their holdings into sectors so you can see how your money is spread across the economy.

questions.prompt: In a market-cap-weighted index fund, bigger companies make up a larger share of the fund.
questions.explanation: Market-cap weighting means a giant like Apple takes up far more of the fund than a small company does.

questions.prompt: A fund puts 7% of its money into its largest holding. If you invest $1,000, how many dollars are in that one company?
questions.explanation: 7% of $1,000 is $70 — the weighting tells you how much of your money sits in each holding.

questions.prompt: Why does one share of a broad fund usually carry less risk than one single stock?
choices: If one company does badly, the others can cushion the blow
Because funds can never fall in value
Because the government insures all funds
Because funds only ever hold winning stocks
questions.explanation: Spreading money across many companies means no single failure can wipe you out — that's the power of diversification.

questions.prompt: What can you typically learn from a fund's fact sheet? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Its top holdings
How it's split across sectors
Exactly what it will be worth next year
Its expense ratio
questions.explanation: A fact sheet shows holdings, sector breakdown, and fees — but no one can promise a future price.

questions.prompt: Owning one share of a diversified fund means you indirectly own tiny slices of many different companies at once.
questions.explanation: That single share represents a sliver of every company in the fund — one purchase, many businesses.

questions.prompt: What is an expense ratio?
choices: A fund's yearly fee, shown as a percent of the money you have invested
The return the fund guarantees you
A one-time fee just to open an account
The tax you owe on your gains
questions.explanation: The expense ratio is the slice the fund quietly takes each year — a 0.10% ratio means $1 per $1,000 invested.

questions.prompt: A fund has a 0.50% expense ratio. On a $10,000 investment, how many dollars does that fee cost you in one year?
questions.explanation: 0.50% of $10,000 is $50 — that's what comes out of your pocket each year for holding the fund.

questions.prompt: Fund A charges 0.05% and Fund B charges 1.05% on a $10,000 balance. How many MORE dollars per year does Fund B cost?
questions.explanation: The 1.00% gap on $10,000 is $100 a year — and that difference compounds against you for as long as you invest.

questions.prompt: A 1% annual fee sounds tiny, but over decades it can quietly cost you tens of thousands of dollars in lost growth.
questions.explanation: Every dollar taken in fees is also a dollar that never compounds for you, so small fees snowball over a lifetime.

questions.prompt: Order these funds from cheapest to most expensive by expense ratio.
questions.explanation: Lower expense ratios keep more of your money invested and compounding — cheaper is usually better.

questions.prompt: Why do fees hurt more the longer you invest?
choices: You lose the fee AND all the future growth that money could have earned — year after year
Fees only apply during the first year
Fees make the market go up
Fees are fully refunded at retirement
questions.explanation: Fees don't just take money once; they steal the compounding that money would have produced for decades.

questions.prompt: Which habits help you keep investing costs low? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Choosing low-expense-ratio index funds
Avoiding funds with high sales loads or commissions
Trading in and out constantly to chase hot funds
Comparing expense ratios before you buy
questions.explanation: Low ratios, avoiding loads, and comparing costs all help; constant trading usually adds fees and taxes.

questions.prompt: What is a robo-advisor?
choices: An online service that automatically builds and manages a diversified portfolio for you, usually for a low fee
A robot that visits your house to give advice
A stock that only trades on weekends
A government retirement program
questions.explanation: Robo-advisors use software to pick low-cost funds, rebalance, and manage your mix so you don't have to do it by hand.

questions.prompt: What is a target-date fund?
choices: A fund that automatically shifts from riskier to safer investments as your target year approaches
A fund you're forced to sell on one specific date
A fund that holds just one stock
A fund that charges no fees ever
questions.explanation: A target-date fund starts aggressive and gradually turns conservative as your goal year — like retirement — nears.

questions.prompt: A target-date fund labeled '2065' is designed for someone planning to retire around the year 2065.
questions.explanation: The year in the name is the rough target — the fund adjusts its risk on a glide path toward that date.

questions.prompt: Match each tool to what it does for you.
pairs: Auto-manages a portfolio based on your goals
Gets more conservative as a set year nears
Tracks a whole market index at low cost
Invests a set amount on a schedule for you
questions.explanation: Each of these takes a decision off your plate, making it easier to stay invested consistently.

questions.prompt: 'Set and forget' investing works partly because automation keeps you consistent and reduces emotional buy and sell decisions.
questions.explanation: Automating deposits removes the temptation to time the market or panic, which is where many investors trip up.

questions.prompt: Which are real benefits of automated investing? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: It keeps you diversified without constant effort
It removes the temptation to panic-sell
It guarantees a profit every year
It can automatically rebalance your portfolio
questions.explanation: Automation helps with diversification, discipline, and rebalancing — but nothing can guarantee yearly profits.

questions.prompt: You set up an automatic investment of $50 every month. How many dollars will you have invested after one year (12 months)?
questions.explanation: $50 times 12 months is $600 — small automatic amounts quietly add up over time.

questions.prompt: Over the long run, most actively managed funds tend to do what compared with their benchmark index?
choices: Underperform it after fees
Always beat it
Match it exactly
Avoid all risk
questions.explanation: After their higher fees, the large majority of active funds lag the index — the core case for low-cost index funds.

questions.prompt: Which one trades throughout the day at live market prices?
choices: An ETF
A mutual fund
Both price only once a year
Neither can be traded
questions.explanation: ETFs trade all day like stocks, while mutual funds price just once daily after the close.

questions.prompt: A fund charges a 0.30% expense ratio. On a $5,000 investment, what is the annual fee in dollars?
questions.explanation: 0.30% of $5,000 is $15 — the fund's yearly cut of your money.

questions.prompt: A mutual fund order fills at the day's closing NAV, not at the price when you placed it midday.
questions.explanation: All mutual fund trades for a day settle at the same end-of-day NAV, regardless of when you ordered.

questions.prompt: Sort each trait into ETF or Mutual Fund.
items: Priced once per day at NAV
Commonly has a minimum initial investment
Bought and sold via a ticker symbol whenever the market is open
questions.explanation: ETFs behave like stocks with live pricing and a ticker; mutual funds price once daily and often require a minimum.

questions.prompt: Fund X costs 0.10% and Fund Y costs 1.10% on a $20,000 balance. How many MORE dollars does Fund Y charge in one year?
questions.explanation: The 1.00% difference on $20,000 is $200 a year — and that gap compounds against you every year you hold it.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.
pairs: Automatically builds and manages your portfolio
Shifts to safer assets as a set year approaches
A fund's yearly fee as a percent of assets
Owns a whole market index at low cost
questions.explanation: These are the core tools of low-cost, hands-off investing you met throughout the unit.

questions.prompt: Which of these help keep your investing costs low? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Choosing low expense ratios
Using broad index funds
Frequent trading to chase winners
Avoiding high sales loads
questions.explanation: Low fees, broad index funds, and dodging loads keep costs down; constant trading usually adds costs and taxes.

questions.prompt: Order these from least diversified to most diversified.
items: A total world stock index fund
questions.explanation: The more companies (and countries) you hold, the more your risk is spread out.

questions.prompt: One share of a fund costs $400, but you invest $100. How many shares do you own? (Enter as a decimal.)
questions.explanation: $100 divided by $400 is 0.25 — fractional shares let you invest any dollar amount you like.
